newsitem.title: USA: Clinton admin. backs market approach on phone fees.
newsitem.headline: Clinton admin. backs market approach on phone fees.

text.p: The Clinton administration and the Justice Department urged U.S. regulators Thursday to refrain from cutting aggressively the $23 billion a year that long-distance phone companies pay to access the local phone network.

The Commerce Department and the Justice Department's antitrust division, instead, advocated that the Federal Communications Commission for now allow market forces to drive down access charges. They added that the FCC should "prescribe" a rate cut only if competition fails.

Baby Bell phone companies also have advocated such a "market-based" approach. By contrast, long-distance carriers such as AT&T Corp and MCI Communications Corp have urged the FCC to prescribe a sharp cut in the charges they pay the Bells for access to the local network.
"The Bells have dodged a bullet. And the long-distance guys were shooting a bullet and missed," said analyst Scott Cleland of Schwab Washington Research Group.
"This is a don't-rock-the boat, go-slow appraoch. Nobody wants to be blamed for phone rates going up."
The FCC is expected to issue rules within the next two weeks on the matter. FCC Chairman Reed Hundt recently has said he, too, opposes a radical cut in access charges.
Industry officials expect the FCC to restructure the vast web of charges now used to support affordable phone service for all Americans.
The Bells would recover costs influenced by the flow of traffic over phone lines through charges that better reflect customer use, industry officials predicted.
At the same time, costs that are not affected by phone traffic would be recovered through flat monthly fees.
In a letter to the FCC, Assistant Commerce Secretary Larry Irving urged regulators to adopt a market-driven approach, at least for now.

"We believe that consumers will best be served by an approach that gives competition a chance to drive prices down, and that gives the FCC the time it should have to address transition issues," said Irving.
His department's filing with the FCC recommended that the market approach be monitored to ensure it is working.

After January 1 of next year, the FCC should revisit the issue to determine if the market approach is working in the consumers' best interests, the department added. If not, the filing recommends it be replaced with a prescriptive approach.

The Justice Department echoed that view in a letter to the FCC. It urged the FCC to rely on market forces for now to produce pressure for lower access rates, but to consider a prescriptive approach to lower rates in the future if competition does not develop quickly enough.
